title: Knowledge Check 5: Lessons 21-26
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 21-26 of the hermes-consultant series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson about monitoring and observability, what is the central focus?
options: A history of monitoring dashboards
The craft of knowing when an agent is quietly failing, by separating loud from quiet failures and watching the whole fleet and the output
A review of unrelated logging tools
A summary of IT policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches observability as the ability to know what is happening inside a system from outside it, catching the failure no guardrail catches.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A loud failure is the worst kind because it makes the client nervous
Execution history alone proves the output was correct
A quiet failure is one that produces no error at all while the output is simply wrong
Stopping at it ran is enough because it is the important floor
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that quiet failures produce no error while being wrong, and are discovered by the client weeks in, which is the worst place.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A green dashboard is the same as observability
Checking only the star job is sufficient since the others rarely drift
Relying on memory to run the fleet check is reliable
Check the whole fleet on a schedule of your own, and sample the actual output because no status system can catch stale content
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that you check the whole fleet on your own schedule and sample the substance of output, because a status screen will not tell you the numbers are stale.

questions.question: Per the lesson about cost management, what is the central focus?
options: A history of billing software
A review of unrelated spreadsheet tools
Measuring unit cost, putting each piece of work on the right model tier, budgeting recurring load, and pricing the engagement from measurement
A summary of sales policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches how to make the number measured and turn a measured unit cost into a client number that survives the month.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Price the engagement from token math you have not observed
Leave every auxiliary task on auto so summarization runs on the premium model
A five-minute health check should run as an agent job for reliability
Measure a week of real runs before you put a number in a proposal, and never price from a demo
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that a three-run demo tells you nothing, so you measure a week of real runs before pricing.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Model choice is the largest cost difference in a long-running agent
The cache is the biggest cost lever because a mid-session model switch re-reads the whole context at full price
Switching models mid-conversation is always cheap
Inference is the largest cost of the engagement and should drive the price
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the cache is the biggest single lever, since a switch mid-conversation discards the cached prefix and re-reads the full context at full price.

questions.question: A consultant's weekly report renders perfectly and reports 41 open tickets while the client's data service holds 44. Per the lesson, what was missing?
options: An automated comparison of the report's numbers against the source
A better layout review before delivery
A larger model for the report job
A second weekly digest run to cross-check volume
questions.explanation: The lesson's worked example says the reviewer had opened the file, seen the table, and approved the presentation, while the missing gate was a comparison, the cheapest gate in the engagement.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist the reviewer not be the builder?
options: Because reviewing takes time the builder cannot spare
Because shared context produces shared blind spots, so the author fills in the missing step from memory
Because the builder is usually less senior than the reviewer
Because the docs forbid one agent from holding two roles
questions.explanation: The lesson frames independence as a context property: builder blindness is universal, and a reviewer sharing the builder's session, memory, and assumptions misses the same thing.

questions.question: In the review loop described in the lesson, what is the correct way to reject a candidate?
options: Block the card so the blocked column records the rejection
Reopen the task in triage for a fresh spec rewrite
Comment the criticism and let the implementer decide whether to act
Call kanban_request_changes with a reason so the review run closes as changes_requested and the card returns to the original implementer
questions.explanation: The lesson states that a block is reserved for real external escalation, and that rejecting by blocking burns the signal and drags the card into the block-recurrence path.

questions.question: Per the lesson on troubleshooting in production, what is the first move before changing anything in a live system?
options: Restart the gateway to clear the failure
Preserve the evidence (session logs, state, snapshots) so you can diagnose without destroying what you need to understand
Change the highest-risk config first to see if the symptom clears
Tell the client the fix is done so they stop worrying
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the most destructive instinct is to start repairing immediately, because the first action to fix often destroys the evidence you needed to understand the failure, so you secure the evidence first.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on changing the system?
options: Change several variables at once so the symptom clears faster
Change one variable at a time and prove each change before the next, with a rollback you can actually use
Only change the provider model, never the config
Never change anything without restarting the gateway first
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches the one-variable discipline: each cycle changes exactly one thing, checks the one thing it was meant to change, and only then moves on, so a working fix is something you understand and can reproduce.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the committed-to behavior when a client is affected by a live incident?
options: Go silent while you investigate so the client is not worried
Tell the client only after the fix is verified
Send short updates naming the observed failure, the investigation, the blast radius, and the verification target
Blame the model so the client knows it is not your fault
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the failure mode to avoid is going silent, and a short update that names the symptom, the investigation, the blast radius, and the verification target earns trust by showing work rather than claiming it.

questions.question: Per the lesson on engagement models, what is the real decision behind choosing a pricing model?
options: Which model lets you bill the highest hourly rate
Which model produces a fixed monthly income
Who bears the risk of scope, and who the engagement model matches that risk to
Which model requires the least paperwork to invoice
questions.explanation: The lesson frames the engagement model as the contract over who bears the risk of being wrong about scope, and that risk split is where the money and trust live, not the rate itself.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on when each model fits?
options: Fixed-fee fits work whose scope you have done before and define tightly
Retainer is best for a one-shot implementation
Hourly fits work where the outcome is already clearly defined
Any model works equally for exploration, known outcomes, and ongoing operations
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches fixed-fee where the outcome is well defined and familiar, hourly where scope is genuinely uncertain, and retainer where there is ongoing operational need.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support about a retainer?
options: A retainer is a discount on a bulk block of hours
A retainer should name the set of included work, not just the hours it might cover
A retainer is only for the initial implementation phase
Under a retainer, your incentive is to bill for fighting incidents rather than preventing them
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that a retainer priced as hours in bulk is really hourly, and that a real retainer names the included work. It also teaches the retainer incentive is to prevent incidents so the system stays boring and the relationship renews.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the actual job of a contract or statement of work?
options: To satisfy lawyers and satisfy an administrative requirement
To replace a fragile shared memory of a verbal agreement with something both sides can inspect, so neither side can drift from it quietly
To set the highest possible fixed fee for the work
To list only the deliverables while leaving the exclusions unwritten
questions.explanation: The lesson says the contract's job is not legal posturing but to make the agreement explicit enough that neither side can drift from it quietly, because early drift is cheap and late drift is a betrayal.

questions.question: Which is the biggest single source of scope creep, according to the lesson?
options: A client acting in bad faith to get free work
A retainer engagement that names its included work
Ambiguity: when the work is not defined, no change is out of scope because there is no scope to be out of
A clear change process that makes every change visible and priced
questions.explanation: The lesson states that scope creep is a failure of the handshake, not of the client's character, and that ambiguity is the biggest source because a vague definition invites every addition to be considered in scope.

questions.question: In the worked example, when the client asks the consultant to add weekly summaries, what does the lesson recommend doing?
options: Say yes because the request is small and friendly
Say no because all new work is forbidden under the contract
Absorb the addition silently as part of the existing scope to keep the client happy
Use the change process: name it as new scope, scope it, price it, and add it as a separate bounded piece of work with its own acceptance test
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the consultant says yes through the change process, making the summary a separate bounded deliverable with its own written scope, which keeps the original boundary intact and the client un-surprised.
